summary.en: Motown pop and southern soul are the two main sources of 1960s Black popular music; James Brown is the benchmark between them.
summary.zh: Motown流行乐与南部灵魂乐是60年代黑人流行音乐的两大源头，James Brown则是个中标杆。

body.zh:
Motown流行乐与南部灵魂乐是60年代黑人流行音乐的两大源头，James Brown则是个中标杆。

在本章中，我们会讲到60年代背景下的Motown唱片、Stax唱片以及James Brown的音乐；基本上，也即60年代中期的黑人流行音乐史。讲述这些内容之前，我有必要先阐明几件事情，以便大家在走进这种音乐时能够理解一些重要的议题。首先是一个重要的问题——种族问题，以及它在接下来的内容中扮演了何等角色。种族可能是美国文化中最敏感的议题，所以我们要谨慎措词，不要给人留下错误的印象或者发出错误的信号；尤其是像我这样的人，一个正在讲解黑人音乐的白人。可能有人会说，我这样的人无法真正理解黑人的经历，因而也无法真正理解黑人音乐试图表达的东西。这见仁见智，各人也可以有自己的观点。但我们很幸运。我们无须过分担心这一点，因为我们是站在摇滚乐的立场上观察黑人流行音乐的历史。而且，要说摇滚乐——至少它最初是——主要面向白人青少年，这应该还算公允。如果说摇滚乐有挫败时刻的话，其一或许就是进入70年代时——这会在课程的第二部分提及——摇滚乐与黑人流行音乐变得相互隔离了，好似存在于两个非常不同的世界里。

总之，本章将要讲到的是60年代的黑人流行音乐。但我承认，或者说我提前声明，我们是将黑人流行音乐作为摇滚历史的一部分来讲解。我一直坚称，也希望我的某位学界朋友能够采纳我的建议：我们真正需要的，是一本从其自身角度出发的黑人流行音乐教科书，而不是将Motown、Stax以及James Brown这样的人物塞到摇滚历史中讲解。不过在我们的课程中，站在以摇滚乐为中心的视角上，他们是摇滚史的一个侧面或者说非常有意思的部分。我们不打算以黑人流行音乐为中心，将摇滚、爵士或者西部乡村音乐视为次要的部分。如果真的能将黑人流行音乐放到讨论的中心，那将是一件很棒的事情；那样的一本著作，也会以不同于我的方式来处理本章涉及的内容。

讲到音乐产业中的种族问题，我们已经了解过50年代及其之前的有关故事。当时存在的是所谓“榜单隔离”（chart segregation），实行分隔且不平等的资源分配。节奏布鲁斯被视为主要面向黑人听众的音乐，并未真正获得与主流流行乐相当的资源和关注度；后者则主要面向白人中产阶级听众。我们确实可以从中看到隔离的存在以及若干敏感问题的影子。在流行乐榜单上，有些歌曲是翻唱版本，有些则是从R&B榜单跨界而来；它们之中，部分即是由黑人歌手原唱、最后被白人歌手拿来翻唱的。这在黑人歌手群体中引起了很大的愤恨。它与我国曾经面临的种族问题紧密联系，而且某种程度上，我们如今仍在面临。对美国以外的同学来说，我所谓“我国”，指的是美国。

那么现在就讲一下之前提过的本章重点。新的黑人流行音乐，与英伦入侵、60年代中期的美国回应几乎同期出现，并且存在两个主要的源头。一个是由Berry Gordy Jr.创办、所有的底特律唱片公司Motown。这个厂牌专注于寻找能够跨界到白人听众群体中的黑人流行音乐，它所有的营销工作也都是为了确保黑人流行音乐能够实现这种跨界。Berry Gordy Jr.想要收获尽可能大的听众群体，所以他的策略就是到金钱最多的地方去。而钱最多的地方，就是白人社区。他想确保旗下的艺人对此善加利用。许多批评者认为，努力跨界到白人听众中的举动大有问题，因为它意味着Berry Gordy Jr.和Motown出卖了黑人之本真（blackness）以取悦白人听众。当人们摆出这样的观点时，他们常会将Motown及其跨界倾向和南部的灵魂乐并列对比。方便起见，后者经常直接以孟菲斯的Stax唱片作为代称。相对于Motown，人们认为这些音乐更具备黑人之本真。

我们将会讲述关于Stax和孟菲斯的全部故事，以及Atlantic唱片如何帮助前者分销产品。但真正的问题在于，Stax厂牌的音乐确实比Motown的音乐更“黑”吗？现在你们或许理解了我为何要以种族讨论开始本节，毕竟这是一种非常重要的考虑。另外，它更像是一种批判性的反应。在人们的认知中，Stax的音乐就是比Motown的音乐更“黑”、更忠诚于黑人文化的根源。这是一个有趣的议题，在学界也引起了广泛的讨论。

同时我们还会讲到James Brown。不管你对他有什么意见，都没有人说他出卖了自己的黑人本真。事实上，在很多方面，他是60年代的黑人自尊和黑人身份的标志人物。本章结束时，我们会讲到这个问题：为什么James Brown似乎没有向白人听众妥协、又能跨界取得非凡的成功，而同样追求成功的Motown艺人却会被认为向白人的品味做出了妥协呢？以上就是本章内容的概述。下面是本章的第一节，我们来了解一下Motown的音乐。
body.en:
Motown pop and southern soul are the two main sources of 1960s Black popular music; James Brown is the benchmark between them.

In this chapter we cover Motown, Stax, and James Brown in a 1960s frame—essentially, mid-1960s Black popular music. Before we enter the music itself, a few points need clarifying so the important issues stay visible. First is race, and the role it plays in what follows. Race may be the most sensitive topic in American culture, so we choose words carefully—no false impressions or wrong signals—especially for someone like me, a white person lecturing on Black music. Some will say a person like me cannot truly understand Black experience, and therefore cannot truly understand what Black music tries to express. That is a matter of judgment; people may hold their own views. But we are fortunate not to have to worry overmuch about that here, because we are watching Black popular-music history from a rock-history standpoint. And it is fair enough to say that rock—at least at first—was aimed mainly at white teenagers. If rock has moments of defeat, one may come as we enter the 1970s—covered in Part Two of the course—when rock and Black popular music grow more separate, as if living in two very different worlds.

In short, this chapter treats 1960s Black popular music. I admit—or declare in advance—that we teach it as part of rock history. I have long argued, and hope some academic friend will take up the suggestion, that what we really need is a textbook of Black popular music from its own center, not Motown, Stax, and figures like James Brown shoehorned into rock history. In our course, from a rock-centered view, they are a side of rock history—or a very interesting part of it. We do not put Black popular music at the center and treat rock, jazz, or country and western as secondary. Putting Black popular music at the center would be a fine thing; such a book would handle this chapter’s material differently from me.

On race in the music industry we already know the 1950s and earlier story: so-called chart segregation, separate and unequal resources. Rhythm and blues was treated as music mainly for Black listeners and never truly given resources and attention equal to mainstream pop aimed mainly at white middle-class listeners. We can see segregation and several sensitive issues in that pattern. On the pop charts some records are covers, some cross over from the R&B charts; among them, some were first sung by Black artists and then covered by white artists. That caused deep resentment among Black singers. It ties closely to the racial problems this country has faced—and to some degree still faces. For students outside the U.S., by “this country” I mean the United States.

Now the chapter focus already mentioned. New Black popular music appears roughly alongside the British Invasion and the mid-1960s American reply, and it has two main sources. One is Motown, the Detroit company founded and owned by Berry Gordy Jr. The label concentrates on Black popular music that can cross over to white listeners; all its marketing aims to secure that crossover. Gordy wants the largest possible audience, so his strategy is to go where the money is—and the money is in white communities. He wants his artists to use that. Many critics treat the push toward white audiences as deeply problematic: it means Gordy and Motown sold out Black authenticity (blackness) to please white listeners. When people make that claim, they often set Motown’s crossover impulse against southern soul—often shorthand for Memphis’s Stax. Relative to Motown, that music is said to keep more Black authenticity.

We will tell the full Stax–Memphis story, and how Atlantic helps distribute the product. But the real question is: is Stax’s music really “Blacker” than Motown’s? You may now see why this section opens with race—it is a crucial consideration. It is also something like a critical reflex: in common understanding, Stax simply sounds Blacker and more loyal to Black cultural roots than Motown. That is an interesting issue and widely discussed in scholarship.

We will also cover James Brown. Whatever you think of him, nobody says he sold out his Black authenticity. In many ways he is a marker of 1960s Black pride and Black identity. At chapter’s end we ask: why does James Brown seem not to compromise for white listeners yet still cross over with extraordinary success, while Motown artists chasing success are said to have compromised for white taste? That is the overview. Next: Motown’s music.
